The Spinal Cord & Meninges

The Spinal Cord & Meninges

A complete high-yield walkthrough of spinal cord gross anatomy, meningeal coverings, internal organization, tracts, blood supply, and the clinical correlations examiners love to ask.

Neuroanatomy Batch 44 Dr. Hassan Salaheldeen Exam-Focused

Pairs of spinal nerve roots
42–45 cm
Length of the cord
L1–L2
Adult termination (conus medullaris)

Meningeal layers
Learning Objectives

By the end of this lecture you should be able to:

  • Describe the extent, dimensions, and developmental ascent of the spinal cord.
  • Explain the relationship between spinal cord segments and vertebral levels.
  • Describe the conus medullaris, cauda equina, and filum terminale.
  • List the three meningeal layers and the spaces between them.
  • Describe the external surface features and root formation of the spinal cord.
  • Describe the internal grey and white matter organization, including the major horns, nuclei, and tracts.
  • Describe the arterial and venous supply of the spinal cord.
  • Apply this anatomy to clinical scenarios: Brown-Séquard syndrome, anterior spinal artery syndrome, cauda equina syndrome, and lumbar puncture technique.

Key Definitions

  • Conus medullaris — the tapered inferior end of the spinal cord.
  • Cauda equina — the leash of lumbar and sacral nerve roots below the conus, resembling a horse's tail.
  • Filum terminale — a pial thread anchoring the cord to the coccyx.
  • Denticulate ligament — pial extensions through the arachnoid to the dura that prevent lateral movement of the cord.
  • Cervical & lumbar enlargements — widened cord segments giving rise to the brachial and lumbosacral plexuses.

Gross Anatomy of the Spinal Cord

Extent, dimensions, developmental ascent, enlargements, and termination.

Extent & Location

The spinal cord is part of the central nervous system (CNS), together with the brain. The peripheral nervous system (PNS) consists of the nerves arising from them.

The spinal cord extends from the foramen magnum superiorly to a variable inferior point:

  • Adult: ends at the lower border of L1 / upper border of L2 (level of the conus medullaris).
  • Embryo: the cord initially occupies the whole length of the vertebral canal.
Why Does the Cord "Ascend"? — The Growth Mismatch
As the fetus/child grows, the vertebral column grows faster (in length) than the spinal cord. Because the cord's upper attachment (foramen magnum) is fixed, the cord effectively appears to be pulled cranially relative to the vertebral column — the cord's true lower end ends up higher and higher relative to vertebral levels, finally settling at L1–L2 in the adult.
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 1 — The spinal cord in situ within the vertebral canal. Note the tapering conus medullaris, the descending cauda equina nerve roots, and the thread-like filum terminale anchoring the cord inferiorly to the coccyx.
Fig. 2 — Schematic comparison: in the embryo the cord occupies the full canal; by adulthood, differential growth leaves the cord ending at L1–L2, with lumbosacral roots descending as the cauda equina.
Dimensions
ParameterValue
Length42–45 cm
DiameterConstant, ≈ 1.5 cm (not uniform cylindrical shape — see enlargements below)
Spinal nerve roots31 pairs — 2 consecutive roots (dorsal + ventral) unite to form each spinal nerve
ShapeCylindrical, with grey matter centrally and white matter peripherally (opposite arrangement to the brain)
Regional Divisions & Enlargements

Four Functional Levels

Like the vertebral column, the cord is divided (rostral → caudal) into:

  • Cervical
  • Thoracic
  • Lumbar
  • Sacral

Two Enlargements

  • Cervical enlargement: C4 – T1 → gives rise to the brachial plexus (innervation of the upper limb).
  • Lumbar enlargement: T11 – S1 → gives rise to the lumbosacral plexus (innervation of the lower limb).
⭐⭐ High-Yield The cord is not a uniform cylinder — the cervical and lumbar enlargements correspond exactly to the segments supplying the limbs, which have the richest innervation and largest number of neurons.
Gross Relations

The spinal cord is contained within the vertebral canal, surrounded by the meninges (dura, arachnoid, pia), which are in turn surrounded by the vertebral column, spinal muscles, and ligaments.

Conus Medullaris, Cauda Equina & Filum Terminale

Conus Medullaris

The tapered, cone-shaped inferior end of the spinal cord, located at the level of L1–L2 in the adult.

Cauda Equina

Because the vertebral column outgrows the cord, the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots must travel downward before exiting at their corresponding intervertebral foramina — producing a horse-tail-shaped bundle of roots below the conus.

Filum Terminale

A vestigial remnant of the caudal spinal cord, formed of pia mater, that extends from the conus medullaris to attach to the dorsum of the coccyx. It anchors the inferior end of the cord and spinal meninges.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 3 — Segmental organization of the spinal cord: cervical, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, and coccygeal segments mapped against their corresponding vertebral levels, with root filaments and their exit foramina.
Fig. 4 — Custom schematic: cervical nerve roots (C1–C7) exit above their same-numbered vertebra; because there are 8 cervical roots but only 7 vertebrae, C8 exits below C7 — from T1 downward, every root exits below its corresponding vertebra.
The Rule, Stated Simply

Cervical region (C1–C8)

Each cervical nerve root exits above its corresponding vertebra (e.g., the C1 root exits above the C1 vertebra). Because 8 nerve roots must fit around 7 vertebrae, the C8 root exits below C7 — this is the transition point.

Thoracic, lumbar, sacral regions (T1 and below)

From T1 downward, each nerve root exits below its corresponding vertebra. This helps localize a radiculopathy precisely — e.g., a lesion at "L5" refers to the root exiting inferior to the L5 vertebra.

Dorsal & Ventral Roots → Spinal Nerve

At each vertebral level, 2 consecutive nerve roots (dorsal and ventral) unite to form the spinal nerve fibers. The dorsal and ventral roots meet within the vertebral canal to form the dorsal root ganglion, and from there the nerve fibers pass out through the intervertebral foramen at the vertebral segment corresponding to the spinal segment.

Lumbar Puncture — The Safe Zone
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know A lumbar puncture is performed at the L3–L4 or L4–L5 intervertebral space. Because the spinal cord (conus medullaris) ends at L1–L2 but the subarachnoid space (and CSF) extends further down around the cauda equina, this lower region is a "safe zone" — a needle can be inserted here to sample CSF without risking injury to the spinal cord itself.

The Spinal Meninges

Three fibrous membranes that support, protect, and suspend the spinal cord — continuous with the cranial meninges.

The spinal cord is surrounded by fibrous membranes collectively called the meninges: the dura mater, arachnoid mater, and pia mater — the same three layers that cover the brain, with the same general arrangement and attachments. These membranes support and protect the spinal cord and the spinal nerve roots (including those of the cauda equina) and contain the CSF in which these structures are suspended.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 5 — Cross-section through the spinal cord and its coverings, showing the dura mater, arachnoid mater, pia mater, epidural space, subarachnoid space, denticulate ligament, and the dorsal root ganglion at the level of the intervertebral foramen.

Dura Mater

  • Outermost layer; composed mainly of tough fibrous tissue with some elastic fibers.
  • Continuous with the epineurium of the spinal nerves as they leave the vertebral column.
  • No firm connection to the vertebra.
  • Surrounded by the epidural space (external to the dura), which contains blood vessels supplying the cord, connective tissue, and fat.

Arachnoid Mater

  • A delicate, web-like network of collagen and elastic fibers.
  • The subarachnoid space lies between the arachnoid and pia mater and contains CSF and blood vessels.
  • Function of the CSF here is the same as around the brain: a shock absorber.

Pia Mater

  • A thin layer of elastic and collagen fibers, closely applied ("intimately adherent") to the brain and spinal cord.
  • Gives rise to the denticulate ligament — extends laterally from the pia, through the arachnoid, to attach to the dura, preventing lateral movement of the cord.
  • Continues inferiorly as the filum terminale, anchoring the cord's lower end.
Spaces at a Glance
SpaceLocationContents
Epidural spaceExternal to the dura materBlood vessels, connective tissue, fat — no firm attachment to vertebra
Subarachnoid spaceBetween arachnoid and pia materCSF, blood vessels; the site sampled during lumbar puncture
⭐ High-Yield The denticulate ligament (lateral, side-to-side anchoring) and the filum terminale (inferior anchoring) both arise from the pia mater and together prevent excessive movement of the spinal cord within the subarachnoid space.

External Surface & Root Formation

The longitudinal grooves of the cord and how root filaments unite into spinal nerves.

Longitudinal Grooves

  • Anterior median fissure — deep groove on the anterior surface.
  • Posterior median sulcus — shallow groove on the posterior surface.
  • Anterolateral sulcus (bilateral) — where ventral root filaments emerge.
  • Posterolateral sulcus (bilateral) — where dorsal root filaments emerge.

Root Formation

From the lateral sulci, a series of root filaments emerge — anteriorly and posteriorly, on each side. These filaments unite to form the ventral root and dorsal root respectively.

The dorsal and ventral roots meet within the vertebral canal, uniting to form the dorsal root ganglion and, ultimately, the mixed spinal nerve, which exits through the intervertebral foramen.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 6 — A spinal cord segment in lateral view: rootlets emerging from the anterolateral and posterolateral sulci unite into the ventral and dorsal roots, which meet at the dorsal root ganglion to form the spinal nerve.
Clinical relevance: The dorsal root ganglion houses the cell bodies of first-order sensory neurons and is a key landmark when localizing radicular (root-level) pain or sensory loss.

Internal Structure — Grey Matter

Unlike the brain, the spinal cord has grey matter centrally and white matter peripherally.

On transverse section, the spinal cord shows white matter in the periphery and grey matter centrally — the reverse arrangement compared with the cerebral hemispheres. In the very center lies the central canal, containing CSF (it is continuous with the fourth ventricle above, part of the same CSF pathway as the lateral → third → fourth ventricles).

A single layer of ependymal cells lines the central canal. Surrounding this is the grey matter, containing cell bodies and nuclei, classically described as shaped like the letter "H" or a butterfly.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 7 — Transverse section: central canal surrounded by "H"/butterfly-shaped grey matter, itself surrounded by white matter organized into dorsal, lateral, and ventral columns (funiculi).

The two wings of the "butterfly" are connected across the midline by the dorsal grey commissure (above the canal) and the white commissure (below/around it). The grey matter on each side is divided into three horns (cell columns): dorsal, lateral, and ventral.

The Three Horns — Click to Expand
Dorsal (Posterior) Horn — Sensory ⭐⭐

Receives the processes of sensory input (first-order neuron axons arriving from the dorsal root ganglion) — found at all spinal levels. Key nuclei:

  • Dorsomarginal nucleus
  • Substantia gelatinosa
  • Nucleus proprius — these three are mainly responsible for light touch, pain, and temperature sensation.
  • Nucleus dorsalis of Clark — transmits unconscious proprioception.

The peripheral receptor → first-order neuron (cell body in the dorsal root ganglion) → relays in the dorsal horn onto the second-order neuron, which carries impulses up toward the cortex.

Lateral Horn — Autonomic ⭐⭐⭐

A bulge present only at specific levels: T1 – L3. Receives/relays sympathetic and parasympathetic impulses.

  • Contains the intermediolateral nucleus, housing preganglionic sympathetic neurons.
  • At T1–T2 specifically lies the ciliospinal center of Budge — provides sympathetic innervation to the eye. Injury at this level → sympathetic disruption to the eye (Horner's syndrome — see Clinical Correlations).
Ventral (Anterior) Horn — Motor ⭐⭐

Contains motor neurons; descending impulses from above relay here. Present at all spinal levels. Key nuclei:

  • Spinal border cells — origin of the ventral spinocerebellar tract.
  • Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2–S4) — injury here → bladder incontinence.
  • Somatic motor nuclei (all levels) — innervate axial and appendicular muscles.
  • Spinal accessory nuclei (C1–C6) — give the spinal root of cranial nerve XI (accessory nerve), which has both a cranial and spinal component.
  • Phrenic nucleus (C3–C6) — supplies the diaphragm.
MNEMONIC
"Sensory Sits Down (Dorsal), Motor Moves out the Front (Ventral)"
Dorsal horn = sensory in; Ventral horn = motor out. Lateral horn (only T1–L3) = autonomic, sitting literally "in between" sensory and motor.
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know C3, C4, C5 keep the diaphragm alive (phrenic nucleus, C3–C6) — a classic exam phrase for localizing high cervical cord injuries that threaten respiration.

White Matter & Tracts

Bundles of myelinated axons carrying ascending sensory and descending motor information.

White matter surrounds the grey matter and consists of axons bundled into ascending and descending pathways, organized into 3 funiculi (columns) on each side:

FuniculusLocationMajor contents
Dorsal (posterior) funiculusBetween the dorsal hornsFasciculus gracilis (medial) + fasciculus cuneatus (lateral) — dorsal column pathway
Lateral funiculusLateral to the grey matterLateral corticospinal tract, rubrospinal tract, spinocerebellar tracts, lateral spinothalamic tract
Ventral (anterior) funiculusBetween the ventral hornsAnterior spinothalamic tract and other descending fibers
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 8 — Cross-sectional map of the major tracts: dorsal columns (gracilis & cuneatus) posteriorly; lateral corticospinal and rubrospinal tracts laterally; anterior spinothalamic tract anteriorly.
Ascending (Sensory) Pathways — 3-Neuron Chain
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 9 — The classic 3-neuron ascending sensory chain, illustrated from receptor to cortex.

The 3 Neurons, in Order

  • 1st-order neuron — cell body in the dorsal root ganglion; peripheral process reaches the sensory receptor; central process enters the cord and synapses in the dorsal horn.
  • 2nd-order neuron — cell body in the dorsal horn; its axon crosses the midline and ascends to synapse in the ventroposterolateral (VPL) nucleus of the thalamus.
  • 3rd-order neuron — cell body in the thalamus; projects to the primary sensory cortex (postcentral gyrus).
⭐⭐ High-Yield Sequence to memorize: Receptor → 1st-order neuron (DRG) → Dorsal horn (2nd-order) → crosses midline → Thalamus (3rd-order) → Sensory cortex.
Descending (Motor) Pathways
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 10 — The descending motor pathway: from the cortex (upper motor neuron) down to the anterior horn cell (lower motor neuron).

Upper vs. Lower Motor Neuron

  • Upper motor neuron (UMN): begins in the cortex, descends through the spinal cord to synapse near/at the anterior horn cell.
  • Lower motor neuron (LMN): begins at the anterior horn cell, travels out to the peripheral muscle.

This UMN vs. LMN distinction is central to localizing neurological lesions and is one of the most frequently tested concepts in neurology.

Dorsal column (gracilis/cuneatus) — proprioception, vibration, fine touch Lateral corticospinal tract — voluntary motor Spinothalamic tract — pain & temperature

Blood Supply

Arterial supply from three longitudinal arteries reinforced by segmental vessels, and venous drainage via a plexiform system.

Arterial Supply

Three longitudinal arteries run the length of the cord — from the medulla of the brainstem down to the conus medullaris:

  • 1 anterior spinal artery (runs in the anterior median fissure)
  • 2 posterior spinal arteries (run posterolaterally)

In the upper cervical region, both arise from branches of the vertebral arteries. They travel within the subarachnoid space and send branches into the substance of the cord. At each intervertebral foramen, these longitudinal vessels are reinforced by segmental arteries arising from the:

  • Costocervical trunk and ascending / deep cervical arteries (cervical region)
  • Intercostal arteries (thoracic region)
  • Lumbar arteries (lumbar region)
  • Sacral arteries (sacral region)

In short: the main longitudinal supply travels from above, downward (vertebral artery origin), while segmental arteries reinforce from the side at every level.

🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 11 — Arterial supply: one anterior spinal artery running in the anterior median fissure, two posterior spinal arteries posterolaterally, and segmental arteries entering from the side at each level.
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 12 — Territorial distribution: the anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord (mainly motor pathways); the posterior spinal arteries supply the posterior one-third (mainly dorsal columns / proprioception).
⭐⭐⭐ Must Know Anterior spinal artery thrombosis cuts blood supply to the anterior two-thirds of the cord, where most motor pathways lie → presents with motor weakness, while proprioception and other posterior column functions are spared (posterior third still supplied by the posterior spinal arteries).
Venous Drainage

As with the brain, venous blood ultimately drains into the dural venous sinuses. The pathway:

  1. Spinal veins draining the cord substance terminate in a plexus around the pia mater — six tortuous, often plexiform longitudinal channels.
  2. These drain into the internal vertebral (epidural) venous plexus, located in the epidural space.
  3. The epidural venous plexus passes superiorly through the foramen magnum to communicate with the cranial dural venous sinuses and the vertebral veins.
🔍 Click to enlarge
Fig. 13 — Venous drainage: pial plexus → internal vertebral (epidural) venous plexus → through the foramen magnum → cranial dural sinuses.

Clinical Correlations

Where the anatomy meets the bedside — the associations examiners test most.

Brown-Séquard Syndrome (Cord Hemisection) ⭐⭐⭐ Must Know

Caused by hemisection (lateral half-transection) of the spinal cord — classically from penetrating trauma. Because the dorsal column and corticospinal tract remain uncrossed at the level of injury, while the spinothalamic tract has already crossed near its level of entry, the deficits split ipsilaterally and contralaterally:

Fig. 14 — Custom illustration of Brown-Séquard syndrome: ipsilateral loss of dorsal column function and UMN weakness; contralateral loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic tract has already crossed).
SideDeficitTract involved
Ipsilateral (same side as lesion)Loss of proprioception, vibration, fine touchDorsal column (uncrossed until the medulla)
IpsilateralSpastic weakness / UMN signs below the lesionLateral corticospinal tract (already crossed in the medulla)
Contralateral (opposite side)Loss of pain and temperature, a level or two below the lesionSpinothalamic tract (crosses near the level of entry)
Anterior Spinal Artery Syndrome
Thrombosis of the anterior spinal artery interrupts blood flow to the anterior two-thirds of the cord. Since motor pathways dominate this territory, patients present with bilateral motor weakness below the lesion, with preserved proprioception/vibration (posterior columns, supplied by the posterior spinal arteries, are spared).
Ciliospinal Center of Budge (T1–T2)
Located in the lateral horn at T1–T2; provides sympathetic innervation to the eye. Cord injury at this level disrupts sympathetic outflow to the eye — a key localizing clue (classically associated with Horner's syndrome: ptosis, miosis, anhidrosis).
Sacral Parasympathetic Nucleus (S2–S4) & Bladder Control
Located in the ventral horn at S2–S4. Lesions at this level classically present with bladder incontinence due to loss of parasympathetic control of the bladder.
Cauda Equina Compression
Because the vertebral column outgrows the cord during development, the lower lumbar and sacral nerve roots travel downward before exiting — forming the cauda equina. Compression here (e.g., large central disc herniation) causes specific lower-limb and pelvic symptoms (saddle anesthesia, bladder/bowel dysfunction, bilateral leg weakness) rather than a discrete single-level radiculopathy.
Lumbar Puncture Safe Zone
Performed at L3–L4 or L4–L5. The cord ends at L1–L2, but the subarachnoid space (with CSF) extends further inferiorly around the cauda equina — creating a safe window to insert a needle without injuring the cord.
Upper vs. Lower Motor Neuron Lesion — Quick Comparison
FeatureUpper Motor Neuron (UMN) LesionLower Motor Neuron (LMN) Lesion
Origin of neuronCortex, descending to the anterior horn cellAnterior horn cell, traveling to peripheral muscle
ToneIncreased (spasticity)Decreased (flaccidity)
ReflexesHyperreflexiaHyporeflexia / areflexia
Muscle bulkPreserved (early), disuse atrophy lateMarked atrophy, fasciculations
Babinski signPositive (upgoing)Absent / normal (downgoing)

High-Yield Exam Zone

Every point flagged as exam-critical in this lecture, ranked by importance.

Exam Pearls

⭐⭐⭐ Spinal Injury Levels

Know the exact clinical manifestations expected at C1 vs. C5 vs. T1 lesions — frequently tested with case vignettes.

⭐⭐⭐ Lumbar Puncture Safe Zone

L3–L4 or L4–L5. Cord ends L1–L2, but CSF-filled subarachnoid space continues around the cauda equina.

⭐⭐ Ciliospinal Center of Budge

Lateral horn, T1–T2. Injury → disrupted sympathetic supply to the eye → Horner's syndrome.

⭐⭐⭐ UMN vs. LMN

UMN starts in cortex, descends to synapse in the cord. LMN starts at the anterior horn cell, travels to muscle.

⭐⭐⭐ Brown-Séquard Syndrome

Hemisection → ipsilateral dorsal column + corticospinal deficits; contralateral spinothalamic (pain/temp) deficit.

⭐⭐ Anterior Spinal Artery Thrombosis

Motor weakness with spared proprioception (anterior two-thirds affected, posterior columns preserved).

⭐⭐ Cauda Equina Compression

Lower-limb/pelvic symptoms from compression of the descending lumbosacral roots below the conus.

⭐⭐ Bladder Incontinence Localization

Sacral parasympathetic nucleus, ventral horn, S2–S4 — lesions here cause bladder dysfunction.

⭐ Spinal Nerve Exit Landmarks

Cervical roots exit above their vertebra (C8 exits below C7); T1 and below exit below their vertebra.

Rapid-Fire Viva Questions
Q: At what level does the adult spinal cord end?

The lower border of L1 / level of L1–L2 (conus medullaris).

Q: Why is a lumbar puncture safe at L3–L4?

Because the cord itself ends at L1–L2, but the subarachnoid space (and CSF) continues down around the cauda equina, so a needle at L3–L4 samples CSF without touching the cord.

Q: Which artery supplies the anterior two-thirds of the cord?

The anterior spinal artery.

Q: Where is the ciliospinal center of Budge and what does it do?

Lateral horn, T1–T2; provides sympathetic innervation to the eye.

Q: What forms the cauda equina?

The lumbar and sacral nerve roots, which must descend within the vertebral canal before exiting at their corresponding foramina, because the vertebral column has outgrown the cord.

Q: What is the filum terminale?

A pial thread anchoring the conus medullaris to the dorsum of the coccyx — a vestigial remnant of the caudal spinal cord.

Q: How many pairs of spinal nerve roots are there, and how are they distributed?

31 pairs total: 8 cervical, 12 thoracic, 5 lumbar, 5 sacral, 1 coccygeal.

Q: What are the ipsilateral and contralateral deficits in Brown-Séquard syndrome?

Ipsilateral: loss of proprioception/vibration/fine touch (dorsal column) and spastic weakness (corticospinal). Contralateral: loss of pain and temperature (spinothalamic), a level or two below the lesion.

Memory & Mnemonics

Quick recall tools for the highest-yield facts in this lecture.

CORD LEVEL
"L1 and Down, LP Is in Town"
The cord ends at L1–L2; lumbar puncture is performed below this, at L3–L4 or L4–L5.
ROOT EXIT PATTERN
"Cervical Climbs Above, Thoracic and below Go Below"
C1–C8 roots exit above their same-numbered vertebra (with C8 the transition exiting below C7); from T1 downward every root exits below its vertebra.
3 MENINGEAL LAYERS
"DAP" — Dura, Arachnoid, Pia
Outer to inner: Dura mater → Arachnoid mater → Pia mater — the same order as around the brain.
GREY MATTER HORNS
"SAM" — Sensory, Autonomic, Motor
Dorsal horn = Sensory · Lateral horn = Autonomic (T1–L3 only) · Ventral horn = Motor.
ANTERIOR SPINAL ARTERY
"Anterior = Action (Motor)"
Anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 (motor-dominant) — thrombosis spares posterior column sensation.
SENSORY PATHWAY ORDER
"1-2-3: Ganglion, Ganglion crosses, Get to Cortex"
1st order (DRG) → 2nd order (dorsal horn, crosses midline) → 3rd order (thalamus) → cortex.

Rapid Revision — One-Page Summary

The last-minute exam-cram version of this entire lecture.

Gross Anatomy

  • Foramen magnum → L1–L2 (adult); embryo occupies whole canal, cord "ascends" as vertebral column outgrows it.
  • 42–45 cm long, ~1.5 cm diameter, 31 pairs of nerve roots.
  • Cervical enlargement (C4–T1) → brachial plexus; lumbar enlargement (T11–S1) → lumbosacral plexus.
  • Conus medullaris (tapered end, L1–L2) → cauda equina (descending lumbosacral roots) → filum terminale (pial anchor to coccyx).

Roots & Levels

  • 31 pairs: 8 C, 12 T, 5 L, 5 S, 1 Co.
  • Cervical roots exit above their vertebra (C8 exits below C7); T1 and below exit below their vertebra.
  • Lumbar puncture safe zone: L3–L4 or L4–L5 (cord ends L1–L2; subarachnoid space continues further down).

Meninges

  • Dura (outer, tough, continuous with epineurium) → Epidural space (vessels, fat) → Arachnoid (web-like) → Subarachnoid space (CSF) → Pia (thin, adherent).
  • Denticulate ligament (lateral anchor) and filum terminale (inferior anchor) both derive from pia.

Internal Structure

  • Grey matter central (H/butterfly shape) around the central canal; white matter peripheral (opposite of brain).
  • Dorsal horn = sensory (all levels); Lateral horn = autonomic (T1–L3 only; ciliospinal center of Budge at T1–T2); Ventral horn = motor (all levels; sacral parasympathetic nucleus S2–S4; phrenic nucleus C3–C6).
  • White matter: dorsal funiculus (gracilis + cuneatus), lateral funiculus (corticospinal, spinocerebellar, spinothalamic), ventral funiculus.
  • Sensory: receptor → 1st order (DRG) → 2nd order (dorsal horn, crosses) → thalamus (3rd order) → cortex.
  • Motor: UMN (cortex → cord) → LMN (anterior horn cell → muscle).

Blood Supply

  • 1 anterior spinal artery (anterior 2/3, motor-dominant) + 2 posterior spinal arteries (posterior 1/3), reinforced segmentally at each level.
  • Venous: pial plexus → internal vertebral (epidural) venous plexus → foramen magnum → cranial dural sinuses.

Clinical Musts

  • Brown-Séquard: ipsilateral dorsal column + corticospinal deficits; contralateral spinothalamic deficit.
  • Anterior spinal artery thrombosis: motor weakness, proprioception spared.
  • Ciliospinal center of Budge (T1–T2) injury → Horner's-type sympathetic eye disruption.
  • Sacral parasympathetic nucleus (S2–S4) injury → bladder incontinence.
  • Cauda equina compression → bilateral lower limb/pelvic symptoms.
